This is a show that explores the values and complexities of race, culture and identity. I'm Sara El Youghun and I'd like to acknowledge that we are broadcasting on unceded Gadigal land. This land has been in the hands of generations of Gadigal custodians for thousands of years before us and it will continue to be in their hands long after us. It's a meeting place for sharing knowledge, stories and song. And we are privileged to be a part of that storytelling today and every day at FBI Radio. I pay my respects to Gadigal Elders past and present. We're broadcasting from Redfern right now, the birthplace of Black theatre in this country and a site for resistance and resilience for First Nations peoples. We honour this in all the work that we do and carry this into our conversation today. Back in the 70s, the Black Power movement paved the way of protest through performance, taking their concerns straight to the street. This reminds me of all the way my people protest. In Syria, there was always a sense of song, chant and dance in the streets. Never fear, just the joy of expression. The story is set against Lebanon's civil war in the 1980s, inspired by her own visits to Lebanon. If you've just tuned in, you're listening to Race Matters on FBi Radio, Kuri Radio, and across the Community Radio Network. I'm Sara El Youghun, and that was Behabbakia Libnan, meaning I Love You, Lebanon, by Farouz. On the other side of my conversation with the wonderful theatre maker, Emily Ayyub. So far, we've spoken together about studying in Western Sydney, her own journey to Lebanon, and her process in bringing her upcoming play, Ruins, to life. You can see Ruins from the 2nd to the 5th of December at the Riverside National Theatre of Parramatta as part of the Heartland Festival 2026. i remember emily was telling me as a performer she was starting to get torn being this sort of vessel for the expression of her grief the simplest things were making her cry compelling her to reactions she didn't quite grasp she didn't know what to do with this feeling so she redirected it to directing as a way of channeling it instead this dedication to share her grief is really inspiring to me because it's changing history through a lens of love. It is a social commentary about what happened to her and her people and telling her own story. I feel like that's invaluable as it's the voice of the people that matters. It's a way for her to share intergenerational memories, forging the path for the future. Through movement, memory is not just spoken. It is embodied and made tangible. Grief asks us to come together, to watch and to listen, to move and be moved. There is an immense power to that. A lot of the time, trauma or grief or these kind of extreme uh sensations that a lot of our um lineages go through even if not directly but just from the um ancestral history a lot of the time it can come out in disassociation or in ways that the west categorizes as almost like not contributing to society and so i think as a theater maker or art director or radio host or um anyone that kind of brings people together for the same purpose it feels like a really productive way to use that let's say zoom out from the psychological and having to bear the crosses of everyone around you I think when you're on stage doing that you are basically channeling energy from your ancestors and people and like that is a very heavy thing to do a very hard thing to hold on your own so i think it's a very beautiful thing to have um gone into directing which feels like it's a creating a container and a community to bring people together i feel like that's such a unique thing to theater particularly in these times it it is a way of gathering people together in one time and space to experience and witness something together so you don't have to hold it on your own as you did on stage in that moment and i feel like the act of watching right like films tiktoks instagram stories whatever it is it's so common to our times but it's so seldom we do this in communion and even rarer that we witness something that is live unfolding with us in the room i wonder how you think about this dimension of theater and why ruins is a place specifically rather than a book, a film, or something else? I mean, theatre is my love language, you know. It's where, as humans, we all come together to take part in, as you say, this communal experience. And it's different every night or every day or every performance, you know. Like, it's never the same again. When we did clowning at Lecoq, our teacher once said to us, you know, What you've done now is really, really funny, but it might not be funny next week. And that's the brutality of theatre as well, is sometimes something really, really works. And then depending on all the other facets that play a part, like the energy of the audience, the energy in the room, the energy of the ensemble, whatever it might be, it changes then and that's pretty unique because it can it has the potential then to become something else and so I think yeah more and more you know we know this like we know how passive we all are on our phones um in in life and you know theater is asking us to sit together and lean forward and lean into something. And I just think as people, we're giving up our time to be in this shared space. So you want it to be extraordinary for the audience. You want it to be, you want it to speak to them in a way that something hasn't before. So the search is really rigorous and yeah, there's nothing quite like it, feeling that shared energy between an audience and an ensemble. My name is Sara El Youghun and today I was thankful to be joined by director and theatre maker Emily Ayub to talk about her abstract approach to theatre and movement in her upcoming play, Ruins. We spoke about studying in Western Sydney and many shared routes, as well as branches, such as the importance of creating space for local Arab communities to see their stories reflected on stage, instead of on the news, while offering all audiences a way into a story about family, culture, loss and belonging.
